transcript.text: Bosch integrated dishwasher showing E:15 and the pump keeps running. Model SMV4HTX31E. I've turned it off and on, still there

On a Bosch dishwasher, E:15 means the anti-flood protection has tripped. The pump and the float switch are probably doing their job. The real question is how the water got there. 1. A small internal leak, such as a sump or pump seal or an internal hose joint dripping into the tray.
2. Foam overflowing. This happens if a drop of washing-up liquid got in, or after too much rinse aid or a switch of detergent.
3. Water getting past the door seal, or being sprayed at the door by a tall item or a spray arm that catches. 1. Turn off the water tap feeding the dishwasher and unplug it or switch off its spur. The pump will stop.
2. Unclip or unscrew the plinth (kickboard) under the furniture door and look underneath with a torch, with towels down. Water on the floor or a wet base tray suggests it's a real leak. A completely dry base points more to a stuck float, which is less likely.
3. Dry the tray as best you can. You can soak it up with a sponge or towels if you can reach it. Otherwise, leave the machine unplugged with the door ajar for a day or two so it dries out. Some people slide the machine out and tip it back to drain the tray. Only do that if you're confident freeing it from the worktop fixings, and get a second person to help.
4. While it's off, look round the door seal for splits or debris, and spin the lower spray arm by hand to check it's not cracked or catching. One important point: once the tray is dry, the error usually clears and the machine may run fine for a wash or two. If the cause is a leak inside, the tray will refill and E:15 will come back. Don't keep re-running it if it does. If the base fills again with no foam involved, the leak point needs finding, typically at a pump or sump seal or a hose underneath. That's normally an engineer job, as the machine has to come out and be partly stripped. Two things would help me narrow it down. With the plinth off, can you see water in the base or underneath? And has any washing-up liquid, extra rinse aid or a new detergent gone in recently?

I can't get the plinth off, it's a continuous kitchen plinth glued at the ends and I'd damage it. Through a gap I can see a little shine of water in the base tray though. No washing-up liquid, I only use tablets. I can't pull the machine out or tilt it either, it's fitted under the worktop.

Seeing water in the base tray settles the main point. The anti-flood float is working properly, and the pump is running because it has detected that water. The switch isn't the fault. The question is where the water is coming from. Foam is unlikely. 1. A small internal leak, such as a sump or pump seal or a hose joint under the tub. This is the most common cause when water ends up in the tray rather than on the floor.
2. Water getting past the door seal, or a spray arm or tall item firing water at the bottom of the door.
3. Less often, a leak inside the inlet hose. Bosch Aquastop hoses are double-walled, so a split inner hose can drain into the base tray instead of onto the floor. 1. Leave the door ajar for 24–48 hours so the tray can dry out. A small amount of water will usually evaporate and the float will drop.
2. While it's drying, look round the door seal for splits or flattened sections. Check the bottom edge of the door. Spin both spray arms by hand and make sure nothing catches.
3. Under the sink, check the tap connection and the drain hose joint at the sink waste with a torch. Drips there point to an external connection. If they're dry, an internal leak or the inlet hose is more likely.
4. Once dry, plug it in and turn the tap back on. Run a short programme with you nearby and a towel at the door. Water at the door edge points to the seal, the door alignment or the loading. If E:15 comes back with the door area dry, it's probably an internal leak. If it returns, stop running it, because each cycle puts more water under your kitchen. At that point it's an engineer job. The machine has to come out from under the worktop, and the pump or sump seals or hoses need checking from underneath. An engineer can usually free a fitted plinth with less risk of damage, or work round it. Tell them about the glued plinth when you book. What did you find at the door seal and spray arms? And does E:15 come back after it has dried?
Door seal looks okay. I haven't checked the spray arms, not sure what I'm looking for. When I left it unplugged for 24h earlier it ran one cycle fine, then E:15 came back.

For the spray arms, you're looking for anything that could squirt water where it shouldn't. 1. Pull out the lower basket. The lower spray arm sits in the middle of the tub floor. Turn it slowly by hand. It should spin freely without wobbling or touching anything.
2. Look along its whole length, top and underneath, especially the seams and the tips. You're checking for hairline cracks, a split along the join, a missing or loose end cap, or a hole that's worn bigger than the others. A split arm sprays a jet sideways, often at the bottom of the door.
3. Do the same with the upper arm under the top basket. With the baskets back in and loaded as you normally would, check that no tall trays, pan handles or utensils hang down into an arm's path.
4. While you're there, glance under the sink with a torch at the tap connection and the drain hose joint. Look for any drip or dampness. If an arm is cracked or catching, that's a good candidate for the cause and a cheap part. If both arms are sound and spin freely, the picture fits an internal leak best. That's the classic pattern of a sump or pump seal, or a hose joint under the tub, slowly refilling the tray. Drying it out only buys a cycle. I'd put that at fairly likely, but not certain until someone sees where the water is coming from. If the arms are fine, I'd stop using it, keep the tap off and book an engineer. Mention the glued plinth when you book, and that E:15 returns after one wash. That lets them come prepared to get the machine out and check the seals and hoses underneath.
ok, I'll have a look at the spray arms. If they're fine I'll book an engineer and mention the plinth. Anything else worth telling them?

Yes, a few things will save the engineer time and may save you a second visit. 1. The model number (SMV4HTX31E), plus the E-Nr and FD numbers from the rating label on the edge of the door. The FD number gives the production date, which helps them bring the right seals and hoses.
2. 3. That after drying for 24 hours it ran one full cycle, then E:15 came back. This tells them it's a steady leak during washing, not a one-off spill.
4. 5. Whether you've seen any water on the floor or under the sink. If it's all in the base tray, that points them to the inside of the machine rather than the plumbing.
6. That it's integrated under the worktop and has a continuous plinth glued at the ends. They may want to allow extra time, or bring something to ease the plinth off cleanly. Also tell them roughly how old the machine is. If it's still under the Bosch guarantee or an extended warranty, book through Bosch rather than an independent. Either way, ask whether the call-out covers finding the leak, and whether they carry common sump and pump seals. Until they come, keep the tap off and leave it unplugged. Let me know how the spray arms look. A cracked or catching arm would be a cheap fix worth trying first. If both are sound, my best estimate is still an internal leak, most likely a pump or sump seal or a hose joint under the tub. That needs the machine out to confirm.
